name: Copenhagen
tagline: Hygge, design and the world's New Nordic kitchen.
whenBlurb: Come May to August for long white-night days and the July jazz festival; December glows for Tivoli's Christmas market, but expect grey and cold the rest of winter.

ourTake.lede: Copenhagen is best taken on two wheels and on foot, at an unhurried pace. Rent a bike, base yourself centrally, and build days around the harbour baths, the food halls and a single great meal rather than a monument checklist. The Little Mermaid is a five-minute disappointment everyone queues for; spend that time in Christianshavn or on a harbour swim instead.
ourTake.comeIf: You care about design, easy cycling streets and one of the best dining scenes in Europe, at a gentle unhurried pace.
ourTake.skipIf: You want warmth, grandeur or a packed sightseeing list; Copenhagen rewards those who slow down, and it is not inexpensive.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Hotel d'Angleterre
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The city's historic grande dame since 1755, a palatial house on Kongens Nytorv, and the definitive Copenhagen address.

items.name: Nimb Hotel
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A romantic Moorish palace inside Tivoli Gardens, just 38 individually designed rooms, with the fairground lights below.

items.name: Nobis Hotel Copenhagen
items.description: A former Royal Danish Academy of Music, reimagined by architect Gert Wingårdh into warm, organic Scandinavian modernism.

items.name: Hotel Sanders
items.area: Indre By / near the Royal Theatre
items.description: Ballet dancer Alexander Kølpin's cinematic 54-room hideaway, nostalgic, layered and quietly glamorous.

items.name: 1 Hotel Copenhagen
items.description: A nature-led harbourfront house on Christianshavn, reclaimed wood, greenery and long water views across to the inner city.

items.name: Villa Copenhagen
items.description: A grand former central post office reborn as a design hotel, soaring public spaces and a heated rooftop pool.

items.name: 25hours Hotel Paper Island
items.description: A playful, art-filled harbour-island hotel on Papirøen, colourful, social and squarely in the design-forward spirit of the city.

items.name: The Park Lane, a Marvelous Hotel
items.description: An elegant townhouse hotel on the Frederiksberg lakes, polished, quiet and a little away from the crowds.

items.name: Nyhavn
items.description: The candy-coloured 17th-century harbourfront is Copenhagen's most photographed stretch, gabled merchant houses, wooden schooners and a canal that once ran to Hans Christian Andersen's front door (he lived at three addresses here). Best walked early morning before the crowds, or seen from the water on a private canal boat.

items.name: Tivoli Gardens
items.description: The world's second-oldest amusement park, open since 1843 and said to have inspired Walt Disney, is far more than rides, think landscaped pleasure gardens, thousands of fairy lights, open-air concerts and a clutch of genuinely fine restaurants. A rare attraction that delights three generations at once, and a magical evening in the Christmas and Halloween seasons.

items.name: The Little Mermaid & Langelinie
items.description: Edvard Eriksen's bronze mermaid, unveiled in 1913 and drawn from Andersen's tale, sits demurely on a rock along the Langelinie promenade. Smaller than most expect, but the waterfront walk past the Gefion Fountain and the royal yacht basin makes the pilgrimage worthwhile; pair it with a private guide who tells the Andersen story properly.

items.name: Amalienborg Palace & the Changing of the Guard
items.description: The Danish royal family's winter residence: four matching rococo palaces around an octagonal square, with the Marble Church closing one vista and the harbour opera house the other. The Royal Life Guards march from Rosenborg and change the guard at noon daily, a crisp, bearskin-hatted ritual that children love. One palace wing is a museum of royal interiors.

items.name: Rosenborg Castle & the Danish Crown Jewels
items.description: Christian IV's fairytale Renaissance summer castle guards the crown regalia and the celebrated crown jewels, diamond, ruby, pearl and emerald garnitures, the emeralds among the finest in the world, in a vault beneath. Above, the Long Hall with its coronation thrones and silver lions; outside, the King's Garden, the city's oldest royal park.

items.name: Christiansborg Palace & the Tower
items.description: The only building on earth housing all three branches of a nation's government, parliament, supreme court and royal reception rooms, Christiansborg also opens its ruins, royal stables and grand hall of Bjørn Nørgaard tapestries. The Tower, at 106 metres the tallest in the city, is free to ascend for a sweeping panorama and a well-regarded restaurant at the top.

items.name: Frederik's Church (the Marble Church)
items.description: A domed rococo church whose 31-metre span is among the largest in Scandinavia, aligned on axis with Amalienborg and the opera house. The interior is serene and gilded; on weekends a guided climb takes you up to the dome walkway for one of the best close-in views over the royal quarter and harbour.

items.name: The Round Tower (Rundetaarn)
items.description: Built by Christian IV in 1642 and one of Europe's oldest working observatories, its charm is the 209-metre spiral ramp, no stairs, that Tsar Peter the Great is said to have ridden up on horseback. A gentle, pram-friendly climb to a rooftop view of the old town's spires and red roofs.

items.name: Strøget & the design shopping quarter
items.description: One of Europe's longest pedestrian shopping streets threads from City Hall Square to Kongens Nytorv, but the real luxury lies in the side streets, the Royal Copenhagen flagship, Georg Jensen silver, Illums Bolighus for Danish design, and Hay House for contemporary homeware. The place to bring home the Scandinavian-design story rather than souvenirs.

items.name: Designmuseum Danmark
items.description: The definitive telling of the Danish design story, from Arne Jacobsen and Hans Wegner chairs to Kaare Klint and modern craft, set in a former rococo hospital. The chair corridor alone is a pilgrimage for design lovers, and the shop and courtyard cafe are worth lingering over. Ideal grounding before you shop the city's showrooms.

items.name: Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek
items.description: Brewing magnate Carl Jacobsen's gift to the city: ancient Egyptian, Greek, Roman and Etruscan sculpture beside a superb hoard of French Impressionists and a full set of Degas bronzes, all arranged around a glass-domed winter garden with palms and a fountain. The garden cafe is one of the loveliest quiet corners in Copenhagen.

items.name: SMK, National Gallery of Denmark
items.description: Denmark's largest art museum spans 700 years, Danish Golden Age masters, Matisse, Emil Nolde and a strong modern wing, in a grand 19th-century building joined to a light-filled modern extension over the sculpture garden. Uncrowded, generous, and free to enter the permanent collection.

items.name: The National Museum of Denmark
items.description: The country's cultural memory under one roof: Bronze Age sun chariots, Viking runestones and hoards, the astonishing Egtved Girl, plus a hands-on children's museum that makes it a genuine multi-generational stop. A private guide can compress the highlights into a rewarding ninety minutes.

items.name: Torvehallerne food market
items.description: Two glass halls by Nørreport station packed with sixty-odd stalls, smørrebrød, fresh fish, Nordic cheeses, coffee roasters, chocolate and produce, much of it organic. The gentlest introduction to new-Nordic eating, with plenty of vegetarian and plant-forward options, and easy to browse with a guide who can point veg-aware families to the right counters.

items.name: Reffen street food market
items.description: Northern Europe's largest street-food market, a 12,000-square-metre waterfront sprawl of shipping-container kitchens serving dishes from dozens of countries, with a brewery, bars and harbour views. Relaxed, family-friendly and full of vegetarian and Indian-friendly choices, a fun, low-key evening away from white tablecloths.

items.name: Kødbyen, the Meatpacking District
items.description: The white-tiled 1930s meat market has become the city's most characterful dining and nightlife quarter, home to natural-wine bars, seafood spots, galleries and buzzing restaurants. Grittier and more local than the old town, it comes alive after dark; a good place to feel the contemporary, creative side of Copenhagen.

items.name: The harbour baths at Islands Brygge
items.description: Copenhagen's harbour is clean enough to swim in, and the Islands Brygge bath, five pools including 50-metre lanes and diving boards, designed by Bjarke Ingels and Julien De Smedt, is where the city cools off in summer. A quintessential, free, sunlit slice of Copenhagen life right in the centre.

items.name: Canal and harbour boat tour
items.description: The single best orientation to the city: an hour on the water past Nyhavn, the opera house, Christianshavn's canals, the Black Diamond library and the Little Mermaid. Private and electric-boat charters are easily arranged for a family or a small group, with a picnic and a guide narrating as you glide.

items.name: Christiania (Freetown)
items.description: A self-governing, car-free community founded in 1971 on a former military site, famous for its murals, workshops, music venues and alternative ethos. Best understood on a guided walk that separates the genuine artistic heritage from the notorious cannabis trade (which the community itself has moved to close); photography is restricted in parts, so tread respectfully.

items.name: Church of Our Saviour spire climb
items.description: The baroque church's black-and-gold spire has an external staircase that corkscrews to the top, 400 steps, the final 150 outside in the open air, wrapping the golden globe. Not for vertigo sufferers, but the reward is a heart-in-mouth 360-degree view over the harbour and old town.

items.name: Botanical Garden & the Palm House
items.description: Ten hectares of landscaped grounds with 27 historic glasshouses, crowned by the cast-iron Palm House of 1874 with its spiral walkway among the treetops. A free, serene green pause beside Rosenborg, lovely for grandparents and children alike, and a quiet counterpoint to the museums.

items.name: Assistens Cemetery
items.description: A leafy 18th-century burial ground that doubles as a much-loved city park, resting place of Hans Christian Andersen, Søren Kierkegaard and Niels Bohr. In summer locals picnic and read under the lime trees along the yellow-walled paths, a peculiarly Danish, unhurried afternoon in the heart of edgy Nørrebro.

items.name: Superkilen park
items.description: A half-kilometre urban park by Bjarke Ingels and Superflex that gathers objects and plants from more than 50 countries, a Moroccan fountain, Japanese cherry trees, a Bollywood-poster sign, benches from Brazil, into a striking red square, black market and green park celebrating the neighbourhood's diversity. A design-world landmark and a genuine slice of multicultural Copenhagen.

items.name: CopenHill (Amager Bakke)
items.description: Bjarke Ingels's audacious clean waste-to-energy plant with a 450-metre dry ski slope, hiking trail and one of the world's tallest climbing walls on its roof. You can ski or ride the year-round Neveplast slope, then take in the harbour panorama from the rooftop bar, architecture, sustainability and a view rolled into one.

items.name: Frederiksberg Gardens
items.description: A romantic English-style landscape park with lakes, canals, a hilltop palace and free-roaming herons, and, thanks to a clever open enclosure, a free view of Copenhagen Zoo's elephants over the water. Grand, leafy and relaxed, it is where well-heeled Frederiksberg strolls on a Sunday.

items.name: Cycling the city
items.description: Copenhagen is the world's most bicycle-friendly capital, with protected lanes, cycle bridges like the sinuous Cykelslangen and more bikes than cars in the centre. A private guided cycle, or a leisurely spin along the harbour on hired e-bikes, is the way locals actually see the city, and utterly safe for confident teenagers and up.

items.name: The Black Diamond & the old town backstreets
items.description: The Royal Library's glossy black waterfront extension is a striking piece of modern architecture with a fine cafe and reading rooms open to visitors. Nearby, wander the medieval Latin Quarter and Gråbrødretorv square, cobbled, café-lined and easy to explore on foot with a guide who knows the hidden courtyards.

items.name: The Cisterns (Cisternerne)
items.description: A cathedral-like former underground reservoir beneath Frederiksberg Hill, now a dramatic, dripping, subterranean venue for a single ambitious contemporary art installation each year. Cool, atmospheric and genuinely unlike anywhere else in the city, a hidden gem for the art-curious.

items.name: Kongens Nytorv & the Royal Danish Theatre
items.description: The city's grandest square, ringed by the Charlottenborg art academy, the historic Hotel d'Angleterre and the Royal Danish Theatre's old stage. It anchors the elegant end of the old town where Strøget meets Nyhavn, a natural gathering point and a fine spot for coffee and people-watching.

items.name: Copenhagen Opera House
items.description: Henning Larsen's monumental opera house sits dramatically across the harbour on axis with Amalienborg and the Marble Church, its vast cantilevered roof a landmark in itself. Catch a performance, or simply admire the maple-and-gold foyer on a guided architecture tour, arriving by boat is the theatrical way.

items.name: Refshaleøen island
items.description: A former shipyard turned post-industrial playground, home to Reffen, harbour saunas, the two-Michelin-star Alchemist, and open-air art and events among the old cranes and warehouses. The most exciting new-Copenhagen quarter, best reached by harbour bus or bike and paired with a swim or a saltwater sauna.

items.name: Nyhavn to Reffen harbour bus (Havnebus)
items.description: The yellow public harbour buses are among the best-value cruises in Europe, a full glide up and down the waterfront past the opera, the library and Refshaleøen for the price of a metro ticket. A gentle, no-fuss way to see the harbour with children in tow.

items.name: Carlsberg City District & the Elephant Gate
items.description: The old Carlsberg brewery quarter, with its famous granite Elephant Gate, has become a design-led neighbourhood of restored industrial halls, cafés and the Home of Carlsberg experience telling the brewing dynasty's story. A pleasant, architecture-rich stroll away from the tourist core.

items.name: Thorvaldsen's Museum
items.description: A jewel-box museum devoted entirely to neoclassical sculptor Bertel Thorvaldsen, its ochre exterior and richly coloured interiors as remarkable as the marble gods and heroes within. Small, uncrowded and deeply atmospheric, a connoisseur's stop beside Christiansborg.

items.name: Grundtvig's Church
items.description: An extraordinary expressionist church built entirely of pale yellow brick, its west front rising like a vast pipe organ. Off the tourist trail in the northern suburbs, it rewards the architecturally curious with one of the 20th century's great church interiors, cool, luminous and utterly still.

items.name: Amager Strandpark & the beach
items.description: A two-kilometre man-made beach island a short metro ride from the centre, with clean Baltic water, dunes and lagoon swimming for children. In summer it is where Copenhagen sunbathes; a surprising, restful contrast to the museums for families who want a beach afternoon.

items.name: Louisiana Museum of Modern Art (Humlebæk)
items.description: Widely rated among the finest modern-art museums in the world, as much for the setting as the art. Low glass galleries ramble through a sculpture park on a cliff above the Øresund, with Giacometti, Calder and Henry Moore framed against the sea. A civilised 35-minute train ride north; the café terrace alone is worth the journey.

items.name: Kronborg Castle, Helsingør (Hamlet's castle)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Kronborg Castle
items.description: The mighty Renaissance fortress guarding the narrowest point of the Øresund is the 'Elsinore' of Shakespeare's Hamlet, and Denmark's most storied castle. Tour the royal chambers, the vast ballroom and the dark casemates where the legendary Holger the Dane sleeps. An easy 45-minute train ride, often combined with Louisiana.

items.name: Roskilde Cathedral
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Roskilde Cathedral
items.description: One of northern Europe's earliest great brick Gothic churches and the burial place of Danish royalty for over 600 years, some 40 kings and queens lie in its ornate side chapels. A living history of Danish architecture in one building, 25 minutes by train and paired naturally with the Viking ships.

items.name: Viking Ship Museum, Roskilde
items.description: Home to five original 11th-century Viking ships raised from the fjord, displayed in a glass hall against the water, plus a working boatyard where reconstructions are built and sailed. In summer you can even take an oar on the fjord, a vivid, hands-on Viking encounter that captivates children and grown-ups alike.

items.name: Frederiksborg Castle, Hillerød
items.description: The largest Renaissance palace in Scandinavia, set romantically across three islets in a lake and now the Museum of National History, its baroque gardens laid out in mirror-perfect parterres. About 40 minutes north by train, arguably the most photogenic of all the Copenhagen castles, and glorious in the gardens on a fine day.

items.name: Dyrehaven & Bakken
items.description: A former royal deer park just north of the city, roamed by hundreds of free deer under ancient oaks, with a hunting lodge on the hilltop and Bakken, the world's oldest operating amusement park (1583), at its edge. A gentle nature-and-nostalgia half-day, easily reached by train and lovely for a family walk.

items.name: Malmö, Sweden via the Øresund Bridge
items.description: The engineering marvel of the Øresund Bridge (of Nordic-noir fame) puts a second country 35 minutes away by train. Malmö offers Calatrava's twisting Turning Torso tower, a walkable medieval core, the Western Harbour waterfront and Swedish fika, an easy, novel add-on for those who want to tick off two Scandinavian capitals' neighbourhood in a day.

items.name: Kastellet (the Citadel)
items.description: One of the best-preserved star-shaped fortresses in Europe, its grassy ramparts, red barracks, church and windmill still an active military site yet open to walkers. A peaceful loop beside the Little Mermaid, best combined into a single waterfront stroll, quietly beautiful at dawn.

items.name: Torvehallerne to Nørrebro food walk
items.description: Beyond the market, Nørrebro and neighbouring Vesterbro hold much of the new-Nordic and immigrant-food story, bakeries, natural-wine bars, and some of the city's best plant-forward and Middle Eastern kitchens. A private food-walking guide can tailor the route for vegetarian or Jain-aware travellers and unlock tables that are hard to book.

items.name: Sankt Peders Bageri & the cardamom-bun trail
items.description: Copenhagen's café and bakery culture is a highlight in itself, from the city's oldest bakery to celebrated spots for the buttery, cardamom-scented cinnamon swirl. A relaxed, low-commitment pleasure that even the most museum-weary teenager enjoys, and an easy vegetarian-friendly indulgence between sights.

items.name: Copenhagen Zoo
items.description: One of Europe's oldest zoos, with a Norman Foster-designed elephant house and an Arctic Ring where you walk through a glass tunnel among polar bears and seals. A dependable, well-run day for younger children, set right beside Frederiksberg Gardens for an easy combined outing.

items.name: Geranium
items.description: Rasmus Kofoed's ethereal, near-vegetarian haute cuisine on the eighth floor above Fælledparken, once ranked the best restaurant in the world.

items.name: Jordnær
items.description: Eric Kragh Vildgaard's intimate, produce-obsessed tasting menu, a modest hotel setting that makes the cooking feel all the more improbable.

items.name: Kadeau Copenhagen
items.description: Nicolai Nørregaard's ode to the Baltic island of Bornholm, foraged, preserved, intensely seasonal Nordic cooking.

items.name: Alchemist
items.description: Rasmus Munk's 'holistic cuisine', a fifty-course, five-act spectacle of food, theatre, science and art under a planetarium dome.

items.name: AOC
items.description: Søren Selin's refined, aromatic tasting menu in the vaulted cellar of a 17th-century mansion, precise and quietly luxurious.

items.name: Koan
items.description: Kristian Baumann's dialogue between Nordic produce and his Korean heritage, a genuinely singular, deeply personal two-star table.

items.name: Kong Hans Kælder
items.description: Classic French technique in Copenhagen's oldest building, a Gothic vaulted cellar that has anchored the city's fine dining for decades.

items.name: Noma
items.description: The restaurant that redefined modern gastronomy under René Redzepi, now reinventing itself again into a seasonal, evolving form.

items.name: Marchal
items.description: Where Nordic produce meets classic French cooking, inside the d'Angleterre, a graceful, grand-hotel room on Kongens Nytorv.

items.name: Alouette
items.area: Indre By / near the King's Garden
items.description: A former industrial building reached by service lift, opening onto a light-filled loft, Nick Curtin's confident, refined cooking.

items.name: Formel B
items.description: A long-standing Frederiksberg favourite, French-Nordic small plates, polished and generous, in an intimate townhouse.

items.name: Jatak
items.description: A buzzy Nørrebro room where Nordic produce meets Asian technique, inventive, fun and full of energy.

items.name: Lille Mølle
items.description: An intimate room by an old windmill on the Christianshavn ramparts, precise, seasonal, quietly excellent Nordic cooking.

items.name: Søllerød Kro
items.description: A thatched 17th-century coaching inn north of the city, classic, elegant cooking in one of Denmark's most beautiful settings.

items.name: Sushi Anaba
items.description: An intimate omakase counter on the Nordhavn waterfront, precise, ingredient-led sushi with a Nordic sensibility.

items.name: Sanchez
items.description: Rosio Sánchez's warm, vivid Mexican cooking, a former Noma pastry chef bringing serious craft to tacos and mezcal.

items.name: Marv & Ben
items.description: Honest, seasonal Danish cooking in a cosy old-town cellar, the kind of well-priced, well-made food the Bib rewards.

items.name: Radio
items.description: Ingredient-driven, sustainable Nordic cooking from a group with deep Noma roots, thoughtful food at a fair price.

items.name: Pluto
items.description: A lively, sociable inner-city bistro, sharing plates, a good wine list and a warm, unpretentious buzz.

items.name: Balthazar Champagne Bar
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN Two-Key, Leading Hotels of the World hotel
items.description: Denmark's original champagne bar, tucked beside the d'Angleterre, an elegant, sparkling perch in the heart of the city.

items.name: Bird
items.description: A warm, vinyl-filled cocktail-and-music bar on Gammel Kongevej, hand-built speakers, considered drinks and an easy local soul.

items.name: Balderdash
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery
items.description: An inventive, culinary-minded cocktail bar in a 1732 townhouse, slow infusions and seasonal produce turned into remarkable drinks.

items.name: Ruby
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery (former Top 50)
items.description: The bar that put Copenhagen cocktails on the map in 2007, a discreet, apartment-like hideaway behind an unmarked door.

items.name: Tata Bar, Hotel Sanders
items.area: Indre By / near the Royal Theatre
items.description: The jewel-box bar inside Hotel Sanders, colonial-nostalgic, low-lit and one of the most beautiful rooms in the city for a nightcap.

items.name: Duck and Cover
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery
items.description: A Vesterbro neighbourhood favourite with a rotating, seasonal Scandinavian cocktail list, relaxed, confident and consistently good.

plan.heading: 3 days in Copenhagen, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Nyhavn and the harbour by small boat, then Amalienborg and the marble church at a slow pace.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Designmuseum Danmark for the chair rooms, then coffee at the Apollo bar in the Kunsthal Charlottenborg courtyard.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Geranium, the three-Michelin-star room above the parkland north of the centre.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A morning at the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek for the Rodin and antiquities, then the winter garden café.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Cycle the lakes and Frederiksberg Garden, or a private tour of the Royal Library's Black Diamond.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Alchemist, the theatrical tasting room in Refshaleøen, booked well in advance.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Louisiana Museum of Modern Art up the coast at Humlebæk, its sculpture park over the Øresund.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at the museum, then the maison houses on Bredgade and Strøget on the return.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at Kadeau, the Bornholm-rooted Michelin room in Christianshavn.

items.name: Indre By (city centre)
items.description: The old core around Nyhavn and Strøget; central and walkable, best for a first stay that wants everything at hand.

items.name: Christianshavn
items.description: Canal-laced and low-key just across the water; suits those who want a quieter, characterful base near great restaurants.

items.name: Vesterbro & Kødbyen
items.description: The former meatpacking district turned dining and nightlife quarter; for travellers who want the city's most current eating and bars.

events.name: Copenhagen Jazz Festival
events.note: Ten days of over a thousand concerts across squares, courtyards and clubs, many of them free and outdoors.

events.name: Copenhagen Cooking & Food Festival
events.note: Northern Europe's largest food festival, with tastings, pop-ups and dinners across the city's restaurants and markets.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in the Indre By or around Nyhavn for the heart of the city; the Danish sensibility is understated and design-led, so dress simply and well, and the best restaurants including the celebrated tables release bookings months ahead.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: You arrive at Copenhagen Airport (CPH) in Kastrup, around 20 minutes by private car to the centre, with a chauffeur meeting you as you clear.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The city is flat, elegant and made for walking or, if you wish to move as the Danes do, cycling; keep a private driver for the drive north to the coast and the art museums.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Connectivity is first-rate; an EU eSIM works throughout as Denmark is within EU roaming, and wifi is fast everywhere.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Danish krone, not the euro; Denmark is effectively cashless so cards and mobile pay cover everything, and tipping is included in prices and not expected.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May to August is warm, bright and best for the harbour and gardens, with June-July at peak daylight; December has design-led Christmas markets but is cold and dark. January-February are the greyest, worth avoiding.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Air India flies direct from Delhi, about 8h15m, in a full business cabin; from Mumbai route via Delhi or a European hub (Lufthansa via Frankfurt/Munich). The Delhi non-stop is the standout convenience; pre-book the Copenhagen airport fast-track for a smooth arrival.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations needed; tap water is excellent and safe. Copenhagen is very safe and orderly; ordinary care around the central station and Christiania is all that's required.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian dining is easy and Copenhagen is notably Jain-aware. Govinda is pure-veg and has catered Jain meals; several Indian kitchens will accommodate onion-garlic-free with notice.
